extracted.intended_audience: educated readers seeking guidance on conversation, disputation, and conduct (gentlemen, students of rhetoric and morals)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and moral guidance on how to conduct conversation and disputation well: when to argue, how to accept correction, what company to seek, and how outward rank and learning affect discourse. Focuses on cultivating a useful, ordered, and truth‑seeking exchange rather than rhetorical parade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer conversation over mere book-learning
rubrics_metrics.description: The most fruitful and natural exercise of the mind is conversation; the study of books is a 'languishing and feeble motion' that heats not, whereas conversation both teaches and exercises at once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek discourse with strong minds and rough disputants because 'his imaginations stir up mine'; conversation stimulates jealousy, glory, and contention and raises one beyond oneself. Beware of learning that merely burdens a weak nature: 'in the hand of some ’tis a sceptre, in that of others a fool’s bauble.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose company and purpose of conversation carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Converse with but few men and for oneself, not as spectacle to amuse the great; one should not treat wit as competitive parade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid turning dispute into entertainment for great persons. Montaigne prefers private, sincere disputation over public displays: 'to do it as a spectacle... is very unbecoming a man of honour.' Choose interlocutors you can learn from and who press you intellectually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value order and method in argument over mere force or subtlety
rubrics_metrics.description: Order and method are more important than force and subtlety in discourse; irregular and disordered disputes frustrate comprehension and are intolerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require that interlocutors stay on subject, as shepherds and shop-boys do, and avoid tumult, prefaces, senseless digressions, or tactical interruptions. When disputes are irregular one should insist on form and method: 'Any one answers too well for me, if he answers what I say.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept contradiction as stimulus, not as affront
rubrics_metrics.description: When contradicted, one should have increased attention rather than anger: contradiction 'raises my attention, not my anger.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat controversy as a common pursuit of truth; welcome reproach and be ready to surrender to superior reasoning provided it is not imperious. Montaigne enjoys being reproved and will 'accommodate myself to my accusers' for civility and improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer and accept correction in the form of conference, not authority
rubrics_metrics.description: One should present oneself to correction especially when it appears as conference and not as imposed authority; we ought to offer ourselves to it rather than evade it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foster environments where admonition is free and mutual. Montaigne contrasts conference (welcomed correction) with authority (resisted correction) and prefers the former as more conducive to improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate a hardy hearing and tolerate blunt speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Fortify and harden your hearing against the 'tenderness of the ceremonious sound of words' and prefer 'stout expressions' among friends so they speak as they think.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value 'strong and manly familiarity'—friendships that are quarrelsome and vigorous—because such sharpness often fortifies and improves thought. Avoid excessive ceremoniousness that silences honest contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not argue with those incapable of relevant inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid disputation with those who 'know nothing to the purpose'—argument with them is futile and disperses the principal subject into petty incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato’s prohibition is cited: ban fools and ill-bred people from dispute. If an interlocutor persistently misunderstands, digresses, or resorts to railing, end the exchange to prevent loss of truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep passions out of disputes; passion usurps reason
rubrics_metrics.description: When passion enters dispute it 'has already confounded his judgment; agitation has usurped the place of reason.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid quarrels where people quarrel with persons not reasons. The angry disputant cannot be reasoned with; the aim should be to secure calm, reasoned exchange so truth can be pursued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim at truth and instruction, not victory or spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose of disputation should be to hunt after truth and to clear the understandings of interlocutors, not merely to win or to display learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne praises Socratic disputation as instructive and criticizes forms that seek victory for its own sake. Prefer forms that 'clear the understandings' and help others perceive their errors rather than theatrical triumphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer submission to sound reason over triumph by another's weakness
rubrics_metrics.description: One should be prouder of a victory over oneself—submitting to an adversary’s force of reason—than of triumphs won through the opponent’s weakness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value internal improvement. Montaigne prefers to 'make myself submit to my adversary’s force of reason' rather than exploit another's faults for personal glory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be tolerant of popular and frivolous opinions to avoid obstinacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Vulgar and casual opinions deserve a hearing; refusing to listen can lead one into obstinacy while hearing them prevents superstition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow space for 'frivolous and extravagant fancies'—they may be inanity, but total refusal to hear them risks becoming intractable. Toleration of oddities can be corrective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer learning of faults by contrariety as well as imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: One may be better instructed by observing fools and what to avoid than by imitating virtuous exemplars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne gives examples (Cato, the harpist sending pupils to hear a bad player) showing that bad examples teach corrective lessons: 'The horror of cruelty more inclines me to clemency, than any example of clemency could possibly do.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Distrust display of erudition that lacks practical judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Academic pedantry and mere recitation of authorities without extracting judgment are worthless; 'learning improves fortunes enough, but not minds' unless handled by a strong nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strip away gowns and Latin—if the learned man cannot make his experience speak and extract conclusions, his show of learning imposes but does not persuade. Avoid appealing to memory in place of reasoned argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate testimony and experience by whether it is distilled into judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: The fruit of experience is not a mere recital of cured cases; experiences must be weighed, sorted and distilled to form usable judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interlocutors appeal to experience ('they have heard, they have seen'), demand that they extract reasons and conclusions, not merely a catalogue of instances. Example: surgeon's cures mean little unless he shows how they inform skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware being misled by outward rank, dress, or fortune
rubrics_metrics.description: Gravity of dress, robe, and fortune often lend reputation to vain arguments and idle words; one should not presume greater sufficiency because of external marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist being 'crushed with examples' from high‑rank persons; judge argument on its merits rather than on who speaks. Megabyzus/Apelles anecdote: silence may inflate perceived greatness that speech later deflates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kingship and great fortune remove the discipline of danger and comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Exemption from danger and competition deprives the great of share in 'honour and pleasure that are consequents of hazard' and places them 'too remote from society' causing isolation and loss of true qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greatness leads to flattery, imitation, and weakened virtues because subjects avoid contending. Examples: princes' followers yield in exercises; gods are ascribed passions to credit courage. This counsels humility and the need for genuine tests and opposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flattery and imitation around the great produce corruption of manners
rubrics_metrics.description: Flatterers and courtiers imitate and authorize a ruler’s vices, making faults fashionable—deafness affected, uncleanliness, disloyalty, cruelty, etc.—thus 'suffer[ing] the soul... to be cauterised.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and resist social contagion of vice near great men; those who surround power tend to adopt its affectations and vices, which undermines genuine virtue and truth in discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-accusation carries more weight than self-praise; use it didactically
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing and accusing one's own imperfections can instruct others by example: 'The parts that I most esteem in myself, derive more honour from decrying, than from commending myself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use candid self-reproach to teach others and to pre-empt vanity; Montaigne argues that a man's accusations of himself are believed whereas his praises are not—a tool of moral pedagogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin reproof with oneself before reproving others
rubrics_metrics.description: Socrates’ precept: if one finds oneself, his son, and a stranger guilty, he should begin with himself and present himself to sentence first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise charity and credibility in reproving others by first acknowledging and correcting one's own faults. This both legitimizes the rebuke and models humility.
